look_here_first: FIND THE TINY BLUNT SPIKELETS: spring panicles are usually open and roughly 3.5–7 cm long, with obovoid spikelets about 1.3–1.6 mm long. Then inspect the often nearly hairless yellowish-green sheath and blade, long basal blade-margin cilia, and conspicuous hair ligule. Autumn branch clusters look unlike spring plants.

best_field_traits: Taxonomy caution: this project uses D. lindheimeri; many FNA/USDA sources treat the same concept as D. acuminatum var./subsp. lindheimeri. Do NOT create a duplicate card.
Basal rosette distinct in suitable season; upper stem leaves commonly 4–9 cm by 4–8 mm, often yellowish green.
Leaf surfaces and sheaths generally glabrous or sparsely hairy; conspicuous long papillose-based cilia near the blade base.
Ligule of hairs, often several millimeters long; compare actual collar, not just the nearby blade-margin cilia.
Open primary panicle about 3.5–7 cm; tiny often obtuse, obovoid spikelets about 1.3–1.6 mm.
Late-season stems develop many small leafy branch clusters (fascicles) and reduced secondary flowering heads.
crew_field_check: Start from the same rooted clump; note spring vs late-season growth.
Expose the collar and photograph the true ligule with a ruler; separate the blade-base cilia from collar hairs.
Measure at least three mature spikelets and examine glumes under magnification.
If collar or spikelet anatomy is absent, label as provisional Dichanthelium sp.
what_to_photograph_for_confirmation: true hair ligule versus long hairs near blade base
one clearly calibrated 1.3–1.6 mm mature spikelet

confused_with: other Dichanthelium species (not yet represented in this learner)
comparisons.key_distinctions: Tiny 1.3–1.6 mm spikelets typically distinguish this concept from the larger-spikeleted D. oligosanthes (~2.9–4 mm) and D. pedicellatum (~3–3.5 mm). Some other D. acuminatum forms have similarly tiny spikelets; compare sheath hair bases, blade margins and ligule under a hand lens. Preserve existing taxonomic concept without re-admitting its alternative name.
